turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $235,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($47,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,080,000, vesting over 4 years
- No sign-on bonus

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.
- As an illustration, not a promise, the recruiter said someone at this level who meets expectations has recently received about $250,000 a year in refresh grants, each vesting over 4 years. If that held, my yearly equity vesting would rise from about $270,000 in year 1 to about $458,000 in year 4, then settle near $250,000/yr after the new-hire grant finishes.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**Negotiate. Don’t walk away yet, but don’t accept the current offer purely for compensation.**

The offer is **reasonable market compensation for a Google L6 PM**, but it is not a compelling “leave a job you like” package:

- Your base would decline by $5,000.
- There is no sign-on or explicit make-whole for the Meta equity you’re leaving.
- Excluding uncertain refreshers, Google’s four-year annualized compensation is about **$552,000**, only **$26,000—or 5%—above** your stated Meta run rate.
- Current self-reported Levels.fyi data puts Bay Area Google L6 PM median compensation around $551,000, meaning this is approximately a median offer, not a premium poaching offer. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

Because you’re happy at Meta and weren’t looking, I would require roughly a **10–15% switching premium**, plus some recognition of near-term forfeited equity.

---

## First, clarify the vesting schedule

There is a significant inconsistency in what you were told.

The recruiter’s illustration—equity vesting rising from $270,000 in year 1 to about $458,000 in year 4—assumes:

- Your $1.08 million new-hire grant vests **25% per year**, and
- Each $250,000 refresher also vests 25% per year.

However, recent reporting says Google new-hire GSUs commonly vest **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, while refresh grants commonly vest evenly over four years. Your actual award agreement controls. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule))

Ask the recruiter, in writing:

> “Can you confirm the exact annual vesting percentages for the $1.08 million new-hire grant, the expected first vest date, and whether the recruiter illustration assumes 25/25/25/25 vesting?”

This changes the year-by-year cash flow considerably, although not the four-year total.

---

## Financial comparison

### If the new-hire grant vests 25% annually

Assuming no stock-price changes, no raises, and target bonus:

| Year | Google without refreshers | Google with $250K annual refresh grants |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $552,000 | $552,000 |
| 2 | $552,000 | $614,500 |
| 3 | $552,000 | $677,000 |
| 4 | $552,000 | $739,500 |
| **4-year average** | **$552,000** | **$645,750** |
| Year 5 steady state | $282,000 | About $532,000 |

The “with refreshers” case is attractive, but it depends on receiving approximately $250,000 every year. Google’s own description says refresh recommendations depend on factors including performance, location and role, with management and compensation-team review. They should not be treated as guaranteed compensation. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

### If the new-hire grant uses 38/32/20/10

| Year | No refreshers | With $250K annual refresh grants |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $692,400 | $692,400 |
| 2 | $627,600 | $690,100 |
| 3 | $498,000 | $623,000 |
| 4 | $390,000 | $577,500 |
| **4-year average** | **$552,000** | **$645,750** |
| Year 5 steady state | $282,000 | About $532,000 |

Under this schedule, the initial offer looks excellent in years 1–2 but creates a major equity cliff. Refreshers become essential rather than merely upside.

### Your Meta comparison

You’ve described two different Meta figures:

- Typical run rate: **$526,000**
- Next 12 months based on $200,000 vesting: **$476,000**

Therefore:

- Against your **usual $526,000 run rate**, Google without refreshers is only $26,000 higher.
- Against your **known next-12-month Meta vesting**, Google is $76,000 higher under even vesting—and much higher if Google’s grant is front-loaded.
- But your Meta figure may also exclude future refresh grants, compensation adjustments or stock movement, so compare both companies on the same assumptions.

The $200,000 Meta vest is not necessarily a separate $200,000 loss on top of your compensation comparison; it is part of what you would earn by staying. Nevertheless, it is entirely legitimate to use it to justify a make-whole request.

---

## What I would ask for

### Opening request

Ask for:

- **Base:** $260,000
- **New-hire GSUs:** $1.35–$1.40 million
- **Sign-on bonus:** $200,000

I would phrase it as a package request, not an ultimatum.

At $260,000 base and $1.35 million in equity, your four-year annualized target compensation before refreshers would be:

- Base: $260,000
- Bonus: $52,000
- Annualized new-hire equity: $337,500
- **Total: $649,500**

That is a meaningful switching premium and reflects that Google approached a satisfied candidate. It is still within the posted base range, which extended to $271,000. Comparable current Google Senior PM postings in the Bay Area show a 20% target bonus and base ranges extending into the high $270,000s. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube%C2%B0ree%3DBACHELORS&distance=50&employment_type=FULL_TIME&gclsrc=aw.ds&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&location=United+States&page=1&q=&sort_by=date&src=Online%2FHouse+Ads%2FBKWS))

The $200,000 sign-on request is ambitious—Levels.fyi currently reports a much lower median sign-on across PM submissions—but your rationale is specific: near-term Meta equity forfeiture and the absence of any need to leave. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

### A good realistic landing point

I would consider this a good outcome:

- **Base:** $250,000–$255,000
- **New-hire GSUs:** $1.25–$1.30 million
- **Sign-on:** $100,000–$150,000

For example:

- $250,000 base
- $50,000 target bonus
- $1.25 million equity = $312,500 annualized
- **$612,500 annualized four-year TC before refreshers**
- Plus a $100,000–$150,000 sign-on

That would give you a roughly 16% recurring premium over your stated $526,000 Meta run rate, before counting any Google refreshers.

### My approximate minimum for a compensation-driven move

Because you like Meta, I would want approximately:

- **$600,000+ annualized over the initial four years, excluding refreshers**, and
- Preferably **at least $100,000 of sign-on/make-whole compensation**.

Possible combinations include:

- $250K base + $1.20M GSUs = $600K annualized; or
- $250K base + $1.30M GSUs = $625K annualized, even without a sign-on.

If Google leaves the package at $235K / $1.08M / $0 sign-on, I would stay at Meta unless the Google role itself is materially more attractive.

---

## How to prioritize the components

If Google says it cannot improve everything:

1. **Base salary:** Ask for at least $250,000. Base compounds through the 20% bonus and future raises.
2. **Initial equity:** Target at least $1.25 million. This is likely the largest practical negotiation lever.
3. **Sign-on:** Seek $100,000–$200,000. It is immediate and not dependent on future refresh decisions.
4. **Start date:** If compensation cannot move, consider delaying your departure until a meaningful Meta vest, provided that doesn’t jeopardize the offer.
5. **Level:** Only raise L7 if the scope and interview feedback plausibly support it. Don’t trade an actionable L6 negotiation for an implausible re-level request.

---

## Suggested message to the recruiter

> I’m very excited about the team and role. At the same time, I’m happy at Meta and wasn’t actively looking, so the decision needs to make sense financially as well as professionally.
>
> My current compensation is approximately $526K annually, and I have roughly $200K of Meta equity vesting over the next 12 months. As currently structured, the Google offer annualizes to approximately $552K before refresh grants, with a lower base and no sign-on. Since refresh grants are discretionary, I can’t treat them as guaranteed when evaluating the offer.
>
> To make the move compelling, I’d like to explore a base of $260K, a new-hire equity grant of $1.4M, and a $200K sign-on or make-whole payment. I understand there may be constraints across individual components, and I’m open to an equivalent combination, but I’m targeting an initial four-year package around $625K–$650K annually before discretionary refreshes.
>
> Could you also confirm the exact vesting schedule for the new-hire grant, the first vest date, and when I would first be eligible for the annual equity-refresh cycle?

If the recruiter pushes for your minimum, avoid immediately giving it. Say:

> I’m flexible on the mix, but the current package is too close to my existing compensation to justify leaving a role I’m happy in. If the team can materially improve the guaranteed four-year value and address the near-term forfeited equity, I think we have a path.

---

## Recommendation

**Negotiate now.**

- **Accept** if Google gets you near the realistic landing package and you prefer the role at least as much as Meta.
- **Stay at Meta** if Google makes only a token improvement, because the current offer provides little guaranteed switching premium.
- **Do not value the $250,000 refresher illustration at face value.** Treat it as upside. The full-refresh scenario is very attractive, but the no-refresh scenario is the appropriate basis for setting your reservation price.

Your strongest leverage is genuine: **you already have a well-paying job you like, Google approached you, and you are fully willing to remain where you are.**

turns.user: Update: I told the recruiter I'd be walking away from about $200,000 of RSUs that would vest in the next 12 months. Final offer: base $240,000, RSUs stay at $1,080,000, plus a $200,000 sign-on bonus. They said this is their best offer. Should I take it?
turns.reply:
## My recommendation: **take it—if you’re at least reasonably positive about the role**

The revised offer crosses the threshold from “too close to Meta” to a **financially compelling switching package**. Google addressed the biggest weakness by fully matching the approximately $200,000 of near-term Meta RSUs with cash.

### Updated economics

Assuming the $1.08 million grant vests evenly:

|  | Google |
|---|---:|
| Base | $240,000 |
| Target bonus | $48,000 |
| Annualized initial RSUs | $270,000 |
| **Ongoing target compensation** | **$558,000** |
| Sign-on | $200,000 |
| **Year-one compensation** | **$758,000** |
| **Four-year total, excluding refreshers** | **$2.432M** |
| **Four-year average** | **$608,000/year** |

Compared with Meta:

- Your normal Meta run rate: **$526,000**
- Google’s ongoing initial-package run rate: **$558,000**, or $32,000 higher
- Google’s four-year average including sign-on: **$608,000**, or $82,000/year higher
- Four-year advantage versus Meta remaining at $526,000: approximately **$328,000**
- Compared with your stated next-12-month Meta compensation of roughly $476,000, Google’s first year is approximately **$282,000 higher**

That four-year premium exists **without assigning any value to Google refresh grants**.

## Why I’d accept

The final package gives you:

1. **Dollar-for-dollar replacement of the $200,000 near-term Meta equity**, in cash.
2. **A modestly higher ongoing package** before refreshers.
3. **Approximately a 16% four-year switching premium** over your current $526,000 run rate.
4. Potential refresher upside—which should remain upside in your analysis, not something you rely on.
5. Base salary preservation: $240,000 at both companies.

This is no longer just a median-ish offer with speculative upside. The sign-on creates meaningful guaranteed initial value and limits the financial cost of making the move.

## The important caveat

After the sign-on is gone, the known package is only **$32,000 per year higher** than your stated Meta run rate. And once the initial $1.08 million grant finishes, Google’s compensation depends substantially on refreshers.

Therefore, this is not an obvious lifetime-compensation upgrade. It is a strong **first-four-years offer**. The decision becomes:

> Is approximately $328,000 of additional nominal four-year compensation enough to accept the role, company, manager and career risk of leaving Meta?

For me, the answer would be yes **provided the Google role is at least neutral professionally**. I would not take it solely for money if you dislike the team, have doubts about the manager, or see substantially worse promotion prospects.

## Confirm these points before signing

Get the following in writing:

- **Exact RSU vesting schedule**, first vest date and vesting frequency.
- **Sign-on payment timing**.
- **Clawback terms**—commonly, repayment may be required if you leave within a specified period.
- Whether the repayment is **prorated or all-or-nothing**.
- Whether termination without cause triggers repayment.
- Whether the sign-on has any special structure, such as installments.
- Your first **refresh eligibility date** and performance-cycle eligibility.
- Your exact team, reporting manager, location and required office attendance.

Also compare the companies’ benefits, including 401(k) match, healthcare costs, ESPP if applicable, PTO and any deferred-compensation differences. Those probably won’t reverse the decision, but they can change the gap by several thousand dollars annually.

## One final tactical move

If they genuinely said “best and final,” I would **not reopen the dollar negotiation**. You got the most important concession. Continuing to press after a full $200,000 addition risks creating friction for little expected gain.

You can still ask for non-compensation accommodations without reframing the offer negotiation:

- A start date after your next Meta vest, if practical
- Written confirmation of the team and manager
- A short signing window extension if needed
- Clarification or improvement of the sign-on clawback language

If you can legally and ethically schedule your start after another meaningful Meta vest without losing the offer, that is valuable—but don’t imply that the $200,000 sign-on was earmarked for equity you would no longer forfeit without being transparent.

## Decision rule

- **Take it** if you would rate the Google role/team at least **7/10** and expect to remain for at least two years.
- **Stay at Meta** if Google is meaningfully worse in role scope, manager quality, work-life balance or promotion prospects.
- Don’t reject it because the package is inadequate. **Financially, the final package is good enough and meaningfully better than the original offer.**

My call based on the facts provided: **accept, subject to reviewing the sign-on clawback and exact vesting terms.**
